function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to actually clone a repository or push changes back to GitHub from here, but I can walk you through exactly what you’d need to do and give you the full content for the files you’ll create.  
Below is a step‑by‑step guide that you can run locally (or in a CI environment) to finish the task.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required files

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Assuming the repo contains a typical Node.js app (e.g. `package.json`, `app.js` or `index.js`), a minimal Dockerfile would look like this:

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
# ------------------------------------
# 1️⃣  Base image
FROM node:18-alpine AS builder

# 2️⃣  Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# 3️⃣  Copy package files & install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# 4️⃣  Copy source code
COPY . .

# 5️⃣  Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# 6️⃣  Start the application
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes the Node runtime.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees reproducible installs.  
> * The app is assumed to listen on port **3000** – adjust if your app uses a different port.

> **If the repo uses a different entry point** (e.g. `index.js` or `server.js`), change the `CMD` line accordingly.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a file called `k8s-deployment.yaml` (or split into separate `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml` if you prefer). Here’s a single‑file example:

```yaml
# k8s-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: ghcr.io/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- replace with your image registry
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: NODE_ENV
          value: production
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **What to change?**  
> * `image:` – point to the Docker image you’ll build/push (GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, etc.).  
> * `replicas:` – adjust the desired number of pods.  
> * `env:` – add any environment variables your app needs.

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      # Checkout the repo
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      # Log in to GitHub Container Registry (replace with Docker Hub if you prefer)
      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

      # Build the Docker image
      - name: Build Docker image
        run: |
          docker build -t ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest .
          docker tag ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}

      # Push the image
      - name: Push Docker image
        run: |
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
          docker push ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:${{ github.sha }}

      # Optional: Deploy to a cluster (requires kubeconfig secret)
      # - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
      #   uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      #   with:
      #     manifests: k8s-deployment.yaml
      #     images: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository }}:latest
```

> **Why this workflow?**  
> * It triggers on pushes to `main`.  
> * It builds and tags the image with both `latest` and the commit SHA.  
> * It pushes to GitHub Container Registry; swap out the login and push steps if you’re using Docker Hub or another registry.  
> * The optional deployment step is commented out – enable it if you have a cluster configured.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s-deployment.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you made any modifications to existing files (e.g. updated `package.json`), add those as well.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will automatically run and build/push your Docker image.

---

### Quick sanity check

1. **Verify the Dockerfile**  
   ```bash
   docker build -t test-nodejs-welcome .
   docker run -p 3000:3000 test-nodejs-welcome
   ```
   Open `http://localhost:3000` to confirm the app is reachable.

2. **Validate the Kubernetes YAML**  
   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f k8s-deployment.yaml
   kubectl get pods
   kubectl get svc
   ```

3. **Check the Actions tab**  
   In GitHub, go to *Actions* → *CI* → *Run workflow* → *View logs* to see the build output.

---

## Recap

| Step | What you did | Why |
|------|--------------|-----|
| 1 | Cloned the repo | Local copy to work on |
| 2.1 | Created Dockerfile | Containerise the Node.js app |
| 2.2 | Created Kubernetes YAML | Deploy the app to a cluster |
| 2.3 | Created GitHub Actions workflow | Automate CI/CD |
| 3 | Added files to Git | Stage changes |
| 4 | Committed & pushed | Persist changes to GitHub |

Feel free to tweak any of the files (e.g. change the base image, adjust environment variables, or add more CI steps). Once you push, the GitHub Actions workflow will take care of building and pushing the Docker image automatically. Happy coding!
